title: Bounded finite module model after polynomial scalar extension
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $n\geq0$ and $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] with its canonical structure map. Use the ordinary module derived categories $D(R)$ and $D(P)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], and ordinary derived extension of scalars $-\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}P$ [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings]. Let $K\in D(R)$ have $H^i(K)=0$ outside a finite interval and every $H^i(K)$ finitely generated over $R$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Then there exist integers $a\leq b$ and a cochain complex $G^\bullet$ of $P$-modules [def-pc-cochain-complex-modules] specialized to the one-point ringed site with structure ring $P$, with $G^j=0$ for $j<a$ or $j>b$ and every $G^j$ finitely generated over $P$, together with an isomorphism
$$Q_P(G^\bullet)\xrightarrow{\sim}K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}P\quad\text{in }D(P),$$
where $Q_P$ is localization of cochain complexes at quasi-isomorphisms. No perfectness of $K$ is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0BZK, lemma-shriek-boundedness, proof: polynomial scalar extension preserves bounded coherent objects; expanded finite-complex representative.

proof.text: Choose integers $l\leq u$ with $H^i(K)=0$ for $i\notin[l,u]$. The Noetherian pseudo-coherence criterion applies to $R$ and $K$, since all their cohomology modules are finite and vanish above $u$. Thus $K$ is pseudo-coherent. Unpacking that definition gives a bounded-above complex $F^\bullet$ of finite free $R$-modules and an isomorphism $e:Q_R(F^\bullet)\simeq K$. Choose $v$ with $F^i=0$ for $i>v$.

Each $F^i$ is flat: after choosing its finite basis, tensoring with it is a finite direct sum, and kernels and preimages in a short exact sequence are computed coordinatewise. Hence the bounded-above flat-complex lemma makes $F^\bullet$ K-flat. Apply derived change of rings on the one-point ringed site for $R\to P$. Apply its computation clause to the identity K-flat resolution $F\to F$: writing $L=-\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}P$ and $E^i=F^i\otimes_R P$, $d_E=d_F\otimes1$, it gives $c:L(Q_R(F))\simeq Q_P(E)$. Thus $h=L(e)\circ c^{-1}:Q_P(E)\simeq L(K)$, since a functor sends an isomorphism to an isomorphism. If $F^i\cong R^{r_i}$ then $E^i\cong P^{r_i}$ via $(z_s)_s\otimes p\mapsto(z_sp)_s$ with inverse $(p_s)_s\mapsto\sum_s e_s\otimes p_s$. Thus $E$ has finite free terms and is zero above $v$.

proof.text: By the polynomial-ring definition, $P$ is the direct sum of copies of $R$ indexed by monomials $x^\alpha$. The mutually inverse coefficient maps $z\otimes\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\mapsto(c_\alpha z)_\alpha$ and $(z_\alpha)_\alpha\mapsto\sum_\alpha z_\alpha\otimes x^\alpha$ identify the underlying $R$-complex of $E$ with $\bigoplus_\alpha F$. Its differential acts coordinatewise. A finite-support tuple is a cycle exactly when each coordinate is a cycle; it is a boundary exactly when each coordinate is a boundary, since preimages can be chosen at its finitely many nonzero coordinates. Consequently $H^i(E)$ as an $R$-module is $\bigoplus_\alpha H^i(F)$, and vanishes for $i<l$ (and for $i>u$).

proof.text: Set $a=l$ and $b=\max(l,v)$. Define $G^i=0$ for $i<a$, $G^a=E^a/\operatorname{im}d_E^{a-1}$, and $G^i=E^i$ for $i>a$, with the induced differential at $a$ and the old differentials above it. The quotient is valid since $d_E^a d_E^{a-1}=0$. The projection $p:E\to G$ is a chain map. At $a$, its cycles are $\ker d_E^a/\operatorname{im}d_E^{a-1}$ and there are no incoming boundaries; in degree $a+1$, the induced map from $E^a/\operatorname{im}d_E^{a-1}$ has the same image as $d_E^a$, while the outgoing differential is unchanged; in higher degrees both differentials are unchanged; below $a$, both cohomologies vanish by step 3. Thus $p$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Images of a finite basis of $E^a$ generate its quotient $G^a$; the other terms are finite free or zero. Therefore $G$ is zero outside $[a,b]$ with finite terms. Localization inverts $p$; the composite $h\circ Q_P(p)^{-1}$ gives $Q_P(G)\simeq K\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}P$.
